## Overview

In Assignment 6 you recognized images with a random forest on raw pixel values. In this short assignment you will use the two ideas behind modern image recognition:

-   **Part A, convolutional neural networks (CNNs):** build a small CNN in PyTorch, compare it with a fully connected network on Fashion-MNIST, and look inside its first layer.
-   **Part B, transfer learning:** reuse ResNet-18, a large CNN already trained on 1.2 million photos, to recognize **your own categories of images** from only a few dozen examples per category.

Part A is short and the same for everyone. **Part B is the main part**: most of the points are for explaining what happens with *your* images.

## What to Submit

Submit the following on Canvas:

| Deliverable | Format |
|---|---|
| Notebook | The completed `assignment11_student.ipynb`, with all cells run |
| Your images | A zip file of your image folder (or a link to it) |

Be ready to show your results in class: in about 2 minutes, show your categories, your accuracy, and one mistake your model made.

The easiest way to run the notebook is [Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com), where PyTorch and torchvision are already installed (upload your image folder to Colab or to Google Drive). On your laptop, install them with `pip install torch torchvision`. Part A takes about 2–4 minutes on a laptop CPU.

## Part A: CNNs on Fashion-MNIST (Questions 1–3, 35 points)

| Question | Topic | Points |
|---|---|:---:|
| 1 | Build and train a CNN with two convolutional layers | 10 |
| 2 | Compare it with a fully connected network (given); count the parameters of a convolutional layer **by hand** | 15 |
| 3 | Look at the learned filters and feature maps, and describe two of **your** filters | 10 |

## Part B: Transfer Learning on Your Own Images (Questions 4–7, 65 points)

1.  Choose **2 or 3 categories** of images you want to recognize, for example dogs vs cats, kinds of food, cars vs trucks, or Bryant buildings. Pick categories you care about.
2.  Collect **at least 30 images per category**. Search engines work well.
3.  Put the images in one folder with **one subfolder per category**:

```
my_images/
    category_1/   img1.jpg, img2.png, ...
    category_2/   ...
```

The notebook reads `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`, `.jfif`, `.webp` and `.bmp` files. Images saved from Google are often `.jfif` or `.webp`.

| Question | Topic | Points |
|---|---|:---:|
| 4 | Turn every image into 512 features with a pretrained ResNet-18 | 5 |
| 5 | Train a classifier on the features; compare it with a random forest on raw pixels; explain the difference **for your categories** | 20 |
| 6 | Explain 3 of your model's mistakes, and what you would change about your data to fix them | 20 |
| 7 | Your own experiment (choose one): fewer images, your own phone photos, or a harder category | 20 |

## How Answers Are Graded

The code is the easy part. Most points are for **explanations that are specific to your results and your images**: what in *that* photo confused the model, why *your* categories are easy or hard to tell apart. An answer that would fit anyone's images gets little credit.

## AI Policy

You may use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot), including to write code. Your explanations must be your own and about your own results. Include a short statement describing how you used AI and anything it got wrong that you had to fix.
